prompt.brief: Design an SLA intelligence platform that computes service-level indicators and error budgets, predicts breaches across dependency chains, and coordinates proactive mitigation.
successSignals: Define SLI event contracts, SLO windows, availability/latency aggregation, exclusions, ownership, and composite dependency semantics.
Compute multi-window burn rates and remaining error budget, forecast breach risk, and avoid false certainty when samples are sparse or delayed.
Separate telemetry ingestion from query/alert paths; make rollups, SLO definitions, and forecast versions reproducible and replayable.
Explain alert deduplication, maintenance windows, remediation approvals, missing data, retention, observability, and degraded dashboards.

functional: Ingest request, latency, error, and dependency events; calculate SLI windows, SLO compliance, burn rates, and error budgets.
Expose service and composite-SLA dashboards with forecast confidence, freshness, drill-down evidence, and historical comparisons.
Create routed alerts and mitigation recommendations, support SLO changes/versioning, replay, and reconciliation after telemetry gaps.
nonFunctional: Update SLO aggregates within one minute and flag high-confidence breach risk at least 15 minutes ahead when evidence supports it.
Scale to millions of telemetry events per minute and large dependency graphs without a single hot key or unbounded synchronous work.
Do not lose committed state; make retries and duplicate events safe.
Degrade safely when downstream workers, caches, or external dependencies fail.
scaleAssumptions: Millions of events/minute across 10k services and 100k dependency edges
Partition by the primary tenant, user, item, or geographic key and isolate hot partitions.
Keep serving state bounded; retain raw events or durable records for replay and auditing.

deepDives.title: Consistency and idempotency
points: Keep the SLA intelligence platform commit authoritative; let derived projections converge with visible version and freshness.
Use idempotency keys, conditional SLA intelligence platform writes, event IDs, and versions so retries and replay are safe.
Return SLA intelligence platform version and observedAt so clients can reason about freshness.

deepDives.title: Partitioning and hot keys
points: Partition SLA intelligence platform by its primary read and write keys, then isolate hot tenants, users, items, or regions.
Bound SLA intelligence platform work with backpressure and queue isolation so one hot key cannot dominate the cluster.
Keep a replay or reconciliation path for SLA intelligence platform projection drift and partial failures.

deepDives.title: Failure and recovery
points: Serve the last acceptable SLA intelligence platform projection or an explicit degraded response when workers fail.
Retain durable SLA intelligence platform records for replay and make each downstream effect independently retryable.
Measure SLA intelligence platform latency, backlog, freshness, error rate, and correctness drift.

tradeoffs.title: Strong consistency versus throughput
tradeoffs.recommendation: Strongly protect the business commit and use versioned eventual projections for high-volume reads.
tradeoffs.caution: Making every derived read synchronous increases coordination and tail latency.

tradeoffs.title: Push versus pull processing
tradeoffs.recommendation: Push bounded events to workers and pull durable snapshots on reads or recovery.
tradeoffs.caution: Unbounded fanout or full scans make bursts and hot keys expensive.

tradeoffs.title: Managed service versus custom control
tradeoffs.recommendation: Start with managed primitives where their limits match the access pattern, then isolate replaceable interfaces.
tradeoffs.caution: Provider defaults do not remove the need for quotas, replay, observability, and data lifecycle design.

commonMistakes: Putting all work on the synchronous request path.
Choosing a data store before writing the access patterns and consistency contract.
Ignoring retries, duplicate events, late data, deletion, privacy, or authorization.
Leaving hot partitions, backpressure, stale reads, and recovery unspecified.
Allowing unbounded requests or exports to compete with normal traffic.

followUps.question: What happens when the primary worker is unavailable?
followUps.answer: Acknowledge only after the durable boundary, serve the last acceptable projection, queue retryable work, and replay or reconcile after recovery.

followUps.question: How would you support a tenfold traffic spike?
followUps.answer: Pre-scale partitions, apply admission control and backpressure, isolate hot keys, cache immutable snapshots, and make freshness degradation visible.

followUps.question: How do you verify correctness?
followUps.answer: Use idempotency metrics, version gaps, sampled source-to-projection comparisons, replay tests, and a shadow rebuild before repair.
